1: Karen O's plea "wait, they don't love you like I love you" was reportedly written about Liars frontman Angus Andrew, her boyfriend then.
2: Jack White's guitar run through a pitch-shifting pedal mimics a bass line, a riff later chanted by football crowds worldwide.
3: Brandon Flowers wrote the jealous, breathless lyrics after discovering his girlfriend cheating at a Las Vegas bar called Crown & Anchor.

5: Thom Yorke's distorted vocals ride a relentless bass line written by him as a teenager, before a chaotic free-jazz horn section erupts.
6: A quiet road-trip meditation that swells into blaring horns and ends with Bridgers and friends screaming into apocalyptic noise.
7: Its choppy, interlocking guitars and Julian Casablancas's muffled croon drew frequent comparisons to Tom Petty's "American Girl."

9: The Sheffield band's first single on Domino went straight to number one in the UK, built on Alex Turner's frantic, wry observations.
10: Nels Cline's long, melodic guitar solo dominates the song's closing minutes, interlocking with harmonized lines from Jeff Tweedy and Pat Sansone.
11: Dave Grohl wrote it during a period when the band nearly broke up, its lyrics about learning to live again.
12: Hayley Williams sings bright, bouncing pop-punk hooks about repeatedly following her heart into heartbreak.

16: Opening with a lone piano note, it follows a dying "Patient" recalling his father's promise, swelling into marching-band theatrics.
17: A single repeating piano figure drives James Murphy's nearly eight-minute reflection on aging, nightlife, and drifting from old friends.

25: Written as encouragement after a fan wrote to the band about feeling out of place among their peers.

30: Rolls along in seven-beat cycles, with Leslie Feist and other collective members trading breathy vocals over shimmering guitars.

33: Restored, extended take on the 2012 breakup ballad that became the longest song ever to top the Billboard Hot 100.

36: Driven by a stuttering riff and Dave Grohl's drumming, it became the band's biggest hit and earned a Grammy nomination.
37: Steady pounding bass drum underpins a song warning that the stories told about sleep and darkness are lies.
38: Grinding blues-rock with slide guitar, produced by Dylan himself under the pseudonym Jack Frost.
39: Glossy synth-pop by the French band evoking Paris at the turn of the twentieth century; widely heard in a Cadillac advertisement.
40: Grammy-nominated thrash assault from an album released on September 11, 2001, with a chorus bitterly rejecting faith.
41: Drum-and-bass breakbeats, distorted guitar and a gospel choir collide in a frantic track whose title abbreviates "Bombs Over Baghdad."
42: A skittering, ska-tinged guitar riff and a brief flute-like keyboard hook drive a song lasting barely over two minutes.

48: Neko Case sings lead on this sugar-rush power-pop track from the Vancouver supergroup's debut, packed with stacked harmonies and handclaps.
49: A chugging, Pixies-style riff and Rivers Cuomo's falsetto carry the lead single that marked Weezer's return after a five-year album gap.
50: Anthony Kiedis's rapid-fire rapped verses alternate with sweet, melodic choruses, John Frusciante's harmonies shaping the album's lusher, pop-leaning sound.
51: Matt Bellamy's falsetto rides a strutting, fuzz-heavy funk riff that drew comparisons to Prince and Franz Ferdinand.
52: Jim James's soaring falsetto and swirling keyboards open the album, celebrating music's power to communicate beyond words.
53: Molly Rankin's wistful vocals float over hazy, jangling guitars in a slow, melancholy song about clinging to a fading relationship.
54: Gritty, stomping guitar backs Harvey's swaggering vocal and the defiant refrain "I can't believe life's so complex."

56: Cabaret strings and accordion frame Brendon Urie's tale of a wedding interrupted by gossip about the bride's infidelity.
57: A loose, droning groove underpins a deadpan account of wandering Queens high and hungry, unable to decide what to eat.
58: Pop-punk about a teenage romance that begins at a concert, with the couple planning to run away together.
59: Hazy guitars and layered vocals carry a protest song about racial injustice and police violence, released amid Ferguson-era demonstrations.
60: Inspired by "Moby-Dick," galloping riffs and roared vocals feature a guest scream from Neurosis's Scott Kelly.

131: A stomping glam beat and a synth line evoking the Doctor Who theme back lyrics urging revolt against bankers and controlling powers.
132: Opening with crackling fireworks, the duo's guitar and drums roar through a toast to youthful nights of drinking and abandon.

138: Fabrizio Moretti's propulsive drumbeat and Nick Valensi's tense guitar solo drive Julian Casablancas's snarling vocals.

148: Ira Kaplan's hushed vocal rides churning, distorted guitar that swells into an extended wash of feedback.

191: Sung by Spencer Krug over pounding drums and keyboards, from a debut produced by Modest Mouse's Isaac Brock.
